History

The pipe screen is one of the oldest small parts in smoking: a disc of mesh or a shaped piece of glass set at the bottom of a bowl so loose material stays put while air passes through. Brass mesh screens were the first common form, sold in bulk packs for a few cents each, because brass is soft enough to press by hand into the curve of a bowl and cheap enough to throw away when it clogs. Stainless steel followed, with a higher melting point and far better resistance to the repeated heating and cooling of daily use. Glass screens came later as a premium form: a daisy or flower shape, moulded in borosilicate, whose raised petals hold the screen above the bowl opening and let air pass around it while blocking particles. Titanium and quartz screens sit at the specialty end of the same family. Sizing settled on the bowl itself: half-inch screens for small pipes, five-eighths and three-quarter inch for most spoon pipes and bong bowls, with the screen matched to the bowl opening so it neither slips through nor sits too high. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage of that change.

The supply in detail

The Pipe Screens (Metal/Glass) works by mesh disc sits at the bottom of the bowl; woven openings pass air and block ash and particles; glass daisy petals hold the screen above the bowl opening and channel air around it It is made from stainless-steel woven mesh, 0.25 mm wire; brass mesh variant; borosilicate glass daisy screen variant, and a common example measures metal mesh screens 15.9 mm (5/8 in) diameter, also 12.7 mm (1/2 in) and 19.05 mm (3/4 in); glass daisy screen 12 mm diameter. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Stainless-steel woven mesh, 0.25 mm wire; brass mesh variant; borosilicate glass daisy screen variant

Dimensions: Metal mesh screens 15.9 mm (5/8 in) diameter, also 12.7 mm (1/2 in) and 19.05 mm (3/4 in); glass daisy screen 12 mm diameter

Mechanism: Mesh disc sits at the bottom of the bowl; woven openings pass air and block ash and particles; glass daisy petals hold the screen above the bowl opening and channel air around it

Use: Press the mesh disc gently into the bowl so it sits flat over the opening, or set the glass daisy in the bowl; replace a mesh screen when it clogs or warps

Care: Rinse glass screens in warm water and dry fully; discard a metal screen that is warped, torn, or clogged beyond cleaning; keep spares in a small tin

Variants: Brass mesh; stainless-steel mesh; titanium mesh; borosilicate glass daisy; glass honeycomb; quartz screens

Materials and design

A pipe screen is a small disc where the material choice is the whole design. Brass mesh is the original: soft, cheap, and pliable enough to press by hand into the curve of a bowl, sold in bulk packs for a few cents each, but it warps and degrades with repeated heating and must be replaced often. Stainless steel is the workhorse: the same woven mesh, but with a much higher melting point and far better resistance to thermal cycling, so it keeps its shape through many heat cycles and does not affect flavour. The standard example here is stainless steel, 0.25 millimetre wire on a 0.8 millimetre pitch, giving an open fraction near one half — enough open area to draw through easily while the wires still block ash and particles.

Build it yourself

There is no genuine do-it-yourself build for a woven pipe screen: weaving stainless mesh to a 0.25 millimetre wire on a 0.8 millimetre pitch needs a loom, and moulding a borosilicate daisy needs a glass furnace, so a home-made screen would be a rough imitation, not a screen. This record says so plainly and gives the closest genuine maker activity instead. The honest home task is fitting and keeping screens: buy a pack of stainless mesh discs in the right size — 15.9 millimetres for most spoon pipes and bong bowls — and shape one to the bowl by pressing it gently over a round object of the same diameter, such as the end of a wooden dowel, so it takes a shallow dome that follows the bowl curve.

3D printing

A pipe screen itself is not 3D-printable: a metal mesh cannot be printed in steel or brass on a home printer, and a glass daisy cannot be printed in borosilicate, so any printed copy would be plastic, would melt in the bowl, and would be unsafe to use. This record says so plainly and gives directions for a printable accessory instead: a screen holder and sizing gauge. Print the holder in PETG, which is tough and survives a pocket: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 3 walls, and 30 percent gyroid infill, printed flat on the bed with no supports.

Use and program

A pipe screen is used by fitting it to the bowl and then forgetting about it until it needs replacing. Press a metal mesh disc gently into the bowl so it sits flat over the opening, following the bowl curve, or set a glass daisy screen into the bowl so its petals hold it just above the opening. The screen then does its job on every draw: it supports the loose material, blocks ash and particles from pulling through into the stem or the water, and leaves enough open area for air to pass. When the draw tightens or the screen warps, lift it out with a poker, discard it, and fit a fresh one; rinse a glass screen in warm water instead and dry it fully before reuse.

Science proof

A pipe screen does two jobs at once and they pull in opposite directions: it must block particles and it must let air through. A metal mesh does this with holes: woven wire leaves square openings, and the open fraction is set by the wire diameter against the wire spacing, so a fine mesh blocks more but chokes the draw. The demo computes that balance for a five-eighths-inch stainless screen, 15.9 millimetres across, with 0.25 millimetre wire on a 0.8 millimetre pitch, giving an open fraction near one half and a few hundred openings across the disc. Brass is the soft original because it bends to the bowl by hand, but it warps and degrades with repeated heat, while stainless steel keeps its shape through many heat cycles because its melting point is far higher and it resists oxidation.

Math proof

The demo computes the supply from its own specification, using the formula A = pi * (d/2)^2, where A is the screen disc area in square millimetres; d is the screen diameter in millimetres. The key figures are screen_diameter_mm = 15.9, wire_diameter_mm = 0.25, wire_pitch_mm = 0.8, daisy_diameter_mm = 12.0. The program applies the formula step by step to those figures and reports each result with its unit, so the reader can repeat the arithmetic with a pocket calculator and get the same numbers within the rounding the program reports.

Use and care

Press the mesh disc gently into the bowl so it sits flat over the opening, or set the glass daisy in the bowl; replace a mesh screen when it clogs or warps Rinse glass screens in warm water and dry fully; discard a metal screen that is warped, torn, or clogged beyond cleaning; keep spares in a small tin Keep the supply dry when it is stored, keep its working surfaces clean, and replace worn parts when they no longer do their job.

Legal note

Legal note: laws on cannabis and cannabis supplies vary by jurisdiction; check local law before buying, possessing, or using this supply.

  • Ganjapreneur — Pipe Screen — https://ganjapreneur.com/vocab/screen/ — A pipe screen is a small mesh or perforated disc placed at the bottom of a pipe or bong bowl to prevent herb, ash, and debris from being drawn through; brass screens are the original and most common type; stainless steel has better durability; glass screens are molded into daisy, flower, or honeycomb shapes.

This record says so plainly and gives the closest genuine maker activity instead. The honest home task is fitting and keeping screens: buy a pack of stainless mesh discs in the right size — 15.9 millimetres for most spoon pipes and bong bowls — and shape one to the bowl by pressing it gently over a round object of the same diameter, such as the end of a wooden dowel, so it takes a shallow dome that follows the bowl curve. Check the fit by setting it in the bowl: it should sit flat over the opening without folding over itself, and it should not slip through. A second genuine maker task is the storage tin: cut a small tin or print a holder (see the 3D printing section), line it with a disc of felt, and keep spare screens in it so they stay flat and clean. Replace a mesh screen the moment it clogs, warps, or tears, because a damaged screen lets ash through and a clogged one chokes the draw, and keep the glass daisy clean by rinsing it in warm water and drying it fully.

demo.code:
"""Demo: pipe screens — The Pipe Screens (Metal/Glass)."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    d = 15.9; wire = 0.25; pitch = 0.8
    area = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2
    open_frac = (1.0 - wire / pitch) ** 2
    open_area = area * open_frac
    holes = int((d / pitch) ** 2)
    daisy_d = 12.0
    daisy_area = math.pi * (daisy_d / 2.0) ** 2
    return {"screen_diameter_mm": d, "screen_area_mm2": round(area, 2), "open_fraction": round(open_frac, 3), "open_area_mm2": round(open_area, 2), "mesh_openings": holes, "daisy_diameter_mm": daisy_d, "daisy_area_mm2": round(daisy_area, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    print(f"screen_diameter_mm: {a['screen_diameter_mm']}")
    print(f"screen_area_mm2: {a['screen_area_mm2']}")
    print(f"open_fraction: {a['open_fraction']}")
    print(f"open_area_mm2: {a['open_area_mm2']}")
    print(f"mesh_openings: {a['mesh_openings']}")
    print(f"daisy_diameter_mm: {a['daisy_diameter_mm']}")
    print(f"daisy_area_mm2: {a['daisy_area_mm2']}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

print3d: A pipe screen itself is not 3D-printable: a metal mesh cannot be printed in steel or brass on a home printer, and a glass daisy cannot be printed in borosilicate, so any printed copy would be plastic, would melt in the bowl, and would be unsafe to use. Print the holder in PETG, which is tough and survives a pocket: use a 0.4 millimetre nozzle, 0.2 millimetre layer height, 3 walls, and 30 percent gyroid infill, printed flat on the bed with no supports. The holder is a disc 40 millimetres across with stepped recesses of 12.7, 15.9, and 19.05 millimetres, so it stores screens of all three common sizes and doubles as a gauge: a screen that drops into the 15.9 millimetre recess and sits flat is the right size for that bowl. Print time (estimate): about 45 minutes for the holder on a standard desktop printer. After printing, clean the recesses with a craft knife, check each recess with a real screen, and sand the rim lightly. Unmodeled factors: wall thickness changes the recess diameters, nozzle settings change stringing in the small steps, printer motion affects the roundness of the recesses, and PETG shrinks slightly as it cools, so measure the printed recesses with calipers before trusting the gauge. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material safely, apply its mechanism cleanly, and survive repeated use without losing its shape. The specification in this record states how the common example meets those three demands, with materials chosen for the job each part does and dimensions that can be measured with a ruler. """The Pipe Screens (Metal/Glass) — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (pipe screens),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for The Pipe Screens (Metal/Glass)."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        d = 15.9; wire = 0.25; pitch = 0.8
        area = math.pi * (d / 2.0) ** 2
        open_frac = (1.0 - wire / pitch) ** 2
        open_area = area * open_frac
        holes = int((d / pitch) ** 2)
        daisy_d = 12.0
        daisy_area = math.pi * (daisy_d / 2.0) ** 2
        return {"screen_diameter_mm": d, "screen_area_mm2": round(area, 2), "open_fraction": round(open_frac, 3), "open_area_mm2": round(open_area, 2), "mesh_openings": holes, "daisy_diameter_mm": daisy_d, "daisy_area_mm2": round(daisy_area, 2)}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()
